name: Yintale Karen
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Shintani, Tadahiko L. A. 2018 (Yintale, ILCAA survey volume; Glottolog doctype phonology_or_text); also Myar Doo Myar Reh 2004 (phonology_or_text)
earlier_scan.note: Print-only Karenic phonologies; tonal language, stress statement not readable online

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2021. Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Sidwell & Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, ch. 18. De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.note: General only: 'Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words' with unstressed atonal minor syllable + stressed full syllable (examples from Pwo, Sgaw, Kayah Li, Kayan); Yintale only named in the list of Karenic groups.

sources.citation: Schiering, René & Harry van der Hulst. 2010. Word accent systems in the languages of Asia. In van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds.), A survey of word accentual patterns in the languages of the world, 509-599. De Gruyter.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: publisher record (DOI); no open copy and no library e-access found (also: publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: Yintale Karen appears only in the genetic classification list (p.584); no StressTyp datum.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2009. Prolegomena to reconstructing Proto-Karen. La Trobe Papers in Linguistics 12. (Yintale as a wordlist column)
sources.note: Only an areal remark: 'Most languages of Southeast Asia are sesquisyllabic (i.e. they have iambic stress)' (sec. 5.2); nothing specific to Yintale.

sources.citation: Kauffman, William G. 1993. The great tone split and Central Karen. MA thesis, University of North Dakota.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Yintale appears only in the classification chart and via Bennett's 1992 unpublished 406-wordlist; stress remarks concern Kayah, not Yintale.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid yint1235 bibliography (3 refs) + CiNii/KAKEN records for LSTCA series
sources.note: Bibliography only: Shintani 2018, Myar 2004, Scott & Hardiman 1900.

sources.citation: Myar Doo Myar Reh. 2004. A phonological comparison of selected Karenic language varieties of Kayah State. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xix+180 pp. (sec. 3.4 'Yintale', pp. 109-133; sec. 4.1 comparison, pp. 134ff)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing. Yintale chapter gives eight syllable types C1(C2)(C3)V1(V2)(C)T, 24 consonants, clusters, rhymes, and 'five contrastive tones in Yintale... high, mid, low, falling and rising' (p.130); no statement on stress, accent, minor/reduced syllables (reduced syllables only 'ignored' in the lexicostatistic algorithm, p.38).

sources.citation: Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds.) 2016. Ethnologue, 19th ed.: Karen, Yintale [kvy] (Wayback capture 2016-08-13)
sources.note: Nothing; 'Reportedly a variety of Western Kayah [kyu]'; dialects Bawlake, Wa Awng; 3 villages, Hpasawng township.

sources.citation: SIL Language & Culture Archives, search for [kvy] (Wayback capture 2015-09-17)
sources.note: Lists only Manson 2009 and Manson 2003 ms 'Karenic Language Relationships: A Lexical and Phonological Analysis'; no Yintale survey or phonology.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2011. The subgrouping of Karen. Paper + handouts, SEALS 21, Kasetsart University, Bangkok. (Yintale data columns)
sources.note: Nothing; comparative reflex tables, Yintale grouped in a Northern/Central cluster.

sources.citation: Shintani, Tadahiko L. A. 2018. The Yingtalay language. Linguistic Survey of Tay Cultural Area (LSTCA) no. 115. Fuchu, Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA). 297 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: The only dedicated modern description of Yintale besides Myar 2004; Shintani's LSTCA volumes open with a phonological introduction (syllable canon, initials, rhymes, tones, often remarks on weak/presyllables) where any stress/accent statement would sit.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2017. The characteristics of the Karen branch of Tibeto-Burman. In Picus Sizhi Ding & Jamin Pelkey (eds.), Sociohistorical Linguistics in Southeast Asia, 149-168. Leiden: Brill.
